name: length-limited-prefix-codes (modified Kraft)
baseline: Package-Merge optimal length-limited Huffman codes, and the MiniZ/JPEG/BZip2 length-limiting heuristics
workload: Computing length-limited Huffman code lengths from the histogram of the first 64 KB of enwik, 100,000 repeats, length limit 12 bits.
claimed_speedup: Modified Kraft (Strategy B) 0.41 s vs Package-Merge 1.17 s, MiniZ 0.58 s, JPEG 0.61 s, BZip2 0.88 s (100,000 runs); output size 62.55% vs 62.51% (Package-Merge) and 62.65% (MiniZ/JPEG). At 8-bit limit 0.24 s vs 0.96 s for Package-Merge. README says it 'outperforms Moffat's Huffman code generator in pretty much all practical use cases' (Moffat unlimited 0.54-0.55 s).
tradeoffs: Code-length construction only (the table-building half of a Huffman coder), not a full encoder or decoder. Strategy B gives slightly longer total output than optimal Package-Merge, worst when the limit nears the lower bound. Single-threaded, plain C with a shared histogram interface that costs some overhead.
caveats: Benchmark code is public but CPU model and compiler flags are missing, so tier C. One dataset (64 KB enwik histogram). Baselines are other length-limiting algorithms from the same repo (MiniZ and JPEG ported by the author), not the upstream libraries run directly. README times are wall times for 100,000 repeats on the author's machine. Last commit June 2021. Hacker News was not the source; found through the GitHub huffman topic page.

name: Glyd
workload: Decompression of an 8.7 GB real-data corpus (logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet); the --max level uses 8-way interleaved Huffman literals and tANS sequences.
claimed_speedup: One core on AWS Graviton3: Glyd default decompresses 3,309 MB/s vs zstd -3 1,425 MB/s and LZ4 1,394 MB/s (ratio 2.82 vs 3.86); Glyd --max 1,571 MB/s at ratio 3.98 vs zstd -3 1,425 MB/s at 3.86. Eight cores: Glyd default 22,707 MB/s vs zstd -3 -T8 1,422 MB/s (Glyd output decodes in parallel; zstd frame decodes on one thread). README summary: 'reads 3-7x faster than zstd on a server'; writes at 0.77x zstd -3 speed.
hardware: AWS Graviton3 c7g.2xlarge and Sapphire Rapids c7i.2xlarge
license: BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 (codec); glyd-store and GPU package under BUSL-1.1
tradeoffs: Rust library with a C ABI, callable from C++. Higher ratio than LZ4 but lower than zstd at default level; compress speed 0.77x zstd -3 and 0.33x in record mode. Large parallel-decode gain needs the parallel-friendly Glyd framing, so output is not a drop-in zstd stream.
caveats: General-purpose compressor, not a standalone entropy coder; likely belongs under general-lossless. Not an entropy-stage-only comparison: wins combine LZ parse, format and parallel framing with Huffman/tANS. The 8-core 'vs zstd -3 -T8' decompress comparison favors Glyd because zstd frames decode on one thread (README says so). README says the full suite and raw rows are in-repo (docs/benchmarks/suite-2026-09-21.md), which I did not open; compiler flags not read. Very new, released in 0.x versions, so tier C pending verifier check of the benchmark files. License is split: codec dual BSD/GPL, store and GPU parts BUSL-1.1.

name: ZipNN
workload: Single-threaded compression of bfloat16 model weights with 256 KB chunks; byte grouping then Huffman or zstd entropy stage in a C extension.
claimed_speedup: ZipNN v0.2.0 compresses at 1120 MB/s and decompresses at 1660 MB/s with ratio 1.51 (66.3% size) vs zstd 785 MB/s compress, 950 MB/s decompress, ratio 1.27 (78.3% size). Version 0.5.4 multithreaded: up to 80 GB/s decompression and 13 GB/s compression on Xeon Platinum 8480+.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (224 cores, two NUMA nodes) for the 80 GB/s figure; hardware for the single-thread table not stated
tradeoffs: Python API with C extension for the Huffman path; specialised to float model weights (bf16, fp16, fp32, fp8) where byte grouping exposes low-entropy exponent bytes. Little or no gain on generic data. Default method is still vanilla zstd with byte grouping of 4; Huffman is one of several selectable methods.
caveats: Gain mostly comes from byte-grouping preprocessing, not from a faster entropy coder; Huffman-vs-zstd split not isolated. The single-thread table has no stated CPU, compiler or flags, and the 80 GB/s figure compares multithreaded ZipNN with no matching baseline row. Not usable directly from C++ without the Python package or extracting the C sources. The LICENSE.txt body names IBM and Drain3 contributors (MIT text); verify the copyright line. The related paper (arXiv 2411.05239) is blocked here and was not opened.
